Battle Engine Aquila Rebuild

The 2003 game, rebuilt one function at a time inside the original, and tested until it plays exactly the same.

About

What this is

I rebuilt the PC game Battle Engine Aquila (Lost Toys, 2003) from its machine code, one function at a time. Each rebuilt function is swapped into the running original game through a small DLL, so the real game keeps working the whole time and any single function can be switched between the original and mine.

I did all of this before I knew the game's source code had been released. That work is kept, unchanged, at the pre-source snapshot.

At a glance

The numbers

4,464of the 4,473 functions Ghidra found, rebuilt and running
102 / 102level tests that play exactly like the original
47 / 47menu tours that match the original pixel for pixel
98of my recorded playthroughs, replayed every test run
30 · 60 · 144frame rates where the original and my rebuild match
Testing

How I tested it

  • A fixed game clock: every frame lasts exactly 1/60 of a second of game time, whatever the PC is doing, so a run plays the same way every time.
  • Recorded playthroughs: I played the levels and recorded every key press and mouse movement. Each test replays one and checks the result, and the game time it happened at, to a tenth of a second.
  • Menu tours: scripted trips through the menus, with screenshots compared pixel for pixel against the original game.
  • Finding the culprit: when a level ends differently, functions are switched back to the original in halves until one function alone explains the difference.
  • A checker that invents its own tests: it runs the original function and mine side by side in an emulator, on made-up inputs, and reports the first difference.
Status

Status

  • 4,464 of the 4,473 functions Ghidra found are rebuilt, and the game plays normally with all of them on.
  • Ghidra missed another 942 small functions, mostly start-up and shut-down code plus mission-script and console commands; they still run as the original's code. Counting them, about 82% of the functions and 90% of the code are rebuilt.
  • About 90% of my rebuilt functions behaved like the original on the first try. About 6% needed fixing.
  • Fullscreen now works on Windows 11, at every resolution from 640x480 to 2048x1536.
Fixes

Problems I found and fixed

Nothing on screen at launch

Windows took the graphics card away from the game at its very first frame. The game waited for it to come back but never asked for it back with Direct3D's reset step, so it waited forever on a black or white window. My version calls the game's own reset routine, which it already had but never used. Fullscreen now starts at every resolution, and Alt+Tab works.

Fullscreen at 65 fps instead of 300

About 500 of my functions are exact machine-level copies of the original. Each time one called the rest of the game, it saved and restored the processor's whole floating-point state, thousands of times a frame. Copying the values as raw bytes, and skipping the save when nothing is in use, took fullscreen from 65 to 225 fps.

Different endings at other frame rates

The game measures its own frame rate from the real clock, and some gameplay code adjusts by "60 divided by the measured rate". For testing, the meter now reports the exact test rate, and the original and my version match exactly at 30, 60 and 144 fps.

Sound making every run different

Mission scripts wait for radio voice lines to finish, and the sound card finishes them on real time. In test runs, sound now follows game time, which exposed two real bugs in my code.

The dropship on level 3.11

The original reads memory it never filled in, picking up whatever ran before. My version of the dropship code used a different amount of memory, so the battle went differently. It now lays out memory exactly as the original does.

Invalid numbers compared the wrong way

When a calculation produces "not a number", the original treated it as equal to zero and my C++ didn't. On level 4.22 that changed when the player fell into the sea. My comparison now behaves like the original's.

Tiny rounding differences

Adding numbers in a different order rounds slightly differently, and over thousands of frames that changed whole battles. I put about 50 functions' sums back in the original's order.

Test runs breaking live games

A test run overwrote a shared Windows controller table, and live games crashed. The test setup now repairs it, and keeps the screen awake so Windows' sleep can't take the graphics away mid-test.

Findings

What the original game does that surprised me

  • It leaks real time. Background loading, voice lines, movies and the frame-rate meter all follow the real clock, so the original doesn't play the same way twice with the same input. With my test switches on, it does: with sound, with movies, and at 30, 60 and 144 fps.
  • It reads memory it never wrote. A few functions pick up leftovers from whatever ran before; one decides when the level 3.11 dive bomber attacks.
  • Its fullscreen never recovers when Windows takes the graphics card away, because it never calls Direct3D's reset.
  • It can't be judged by screenshots alone. Menus name keys through Windows, so a different keyboard layout changes the pictures; my tests now use the US layout for the game only.

The full list, with addresses, is in docs/FINDINGS.md.

Other projects

For other projects

My recordings and test switches can check any version of the game against the original. I built a bridge that turns my recordings into another port's replay format and writes the original game's state every 50 frames as an answer key, so a port can see exactly where it starts to differ.
